narrative:
The model estimated a 76% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, and that high estimated risk is why your law school application was denied. This is not a judgment of your ability or character; it means the information available placed you in a group with a substantially elevated predicted risk of first-time bar failure.

The strongest factor driving the prediction was your third-year class rank: you are in the second decile, while accepted students average near the sixth decile. That gap pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. The second most influential factor was your first-year class rank, where you are in the third decile versus an accepted-student average near the sixth decile; this also pushed toward failure. Your LSAT score of 38 was the third most important factor and was slightly above the accepted-student average of about 37.2, so it pushed toward passing, but it was not enough to offset the academic-rank signals.

To move forward, ask the admissions office for feedback and identify whether a later application could show stronger upper-level academic performance. Consider academic support, additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate record that demonstrates improved ranking, and retake the LSAT only if practice results suggest a meaningful gain. Reapplying after addressing the rank pattern is more likely to change the outcome than reapplying with the same record.
